summary.value: The paper proposes Stylos, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian stylization framework. Given one or more unposed RGB views of a scene plus a single style reference image, Stylos directly predicts a stylized 3D Gaussian scene in a single forward pass, without per-scene optimization or known camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Stylos explicitly separates geometry and style: geometry is inferred by a VGGT-like alternating-attention backbone, while style is injected through a Style Aggregator that applies global cross-attention from the style tokens to all content-view tokens. The paper also introduces a voxel-based 3D style loss: instead of matching style statistics (mean/variance in VGG feature space) per-frame, Stylos fuses multi-view features into a shared voxel grid and aligns those 3D features to the style distribution, which the authors argue enforces cross-view consistency and preserves geometry. Experiments on CO3D, DL3DV-10K, and Tanks and Temples report improved multi-view consistency (LPIPS/RMSE) and competitive perceptual/artistic quality (ArtScore) compared to per-scene stylization baselines such as StyleRF and StyleGS, and include ablations on cross-attention design and style loss variants.

strengths.value:
- Practical significance. Single-forward stylization of an entire 3D Gaussian scene (poses + Gaussians + colors) without per-scene finetuning or known camera parameters could be transformative for content pipelines. This is not just incremental NeRF/3DGS stylization but closer to the real situation, like “instant turn-this-video-into-stylized-3D-assets.”
- Architectural clarity. Clean separation between a geometry backbone and a Style Aggregator branch (global cross-attention conditioning on the style image). The ablation across “frame-only,” “hybrid,” and “global-only” variants is convincing and shows why global conditioning improves structure and texture coherence.
- Breadth of evaluation. The paper reports not only reconstruction-like metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) but also temporal / multi-view consistency metrics (LPIPS & RMSE at different frame gaps) and ArtScore for perceptual “artness,” and demonstrates cross-category and cross-scene generalization.

weaknesses.value:
- 3D style loss justification is empirical. The 3D voxel-statistics loss gives better LPIPS/RMSE consistency, but the paper does not analyze potential side effects such as global color bleeding or loss of local style detail in poorly observed regions. Some intuition or failure-case visualization would strengthen the argument that voxel-statistics matching is fundamentally better than 2D scene-level matching.
- Scalability limits. Although Stylos is advertised as handling up to “hundreds of views,” the scaling experiment shows visible degradation beyond ~32 views per batch (edge artifacts, instability in the Gaussian representation). The method may still be quite useful, but this practical constraint, probably brought by VGGT, should be communicated more prominently.

questions.value:
- Failure cases of the 3D style loss.
Are there any visual failure cases where voxelized style statistics hurt local detail (e.g., oversmoothing, texture bleeding in occluded regions)? Right now we only see success cases and quantitative gains.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for giving our work a positive rating and providing several insightful comments. We have carefully revised the paper and added new experimental results to address the reviewer’s questions. Our responses are as follows.

---

### Responses to Weaknesses

---

> 1. 3D style loss justification is empirical. The 3D voxel-statistics loss gives better LPIPS/RMSE consistency, but the paper does not analyze potential side effects such as global color bleeding or loss of local style detail in poorly observed regions. Some intuition or failure-case visualization would strengthen the argument that voxel-statistics matching is fundamentally better than 2D scene-level matching.

Thanks for recognizing that our proposed voxel-level 3D style loss yields improved multi-view consistency, and for raising a valuable point regarding the motivation behind this design.

First, our 3D style loss is view-independent because the style statistics are computed in the shared 3D voxel space, neither in the simple image plane nor in the 2D-based multi-view scene. Features from all views are first mapped to their corresponding 3D locations and fused in the voxel grid. Each voxel, therefore, aggregates appearance information from all valid observations, and the style loss is applied to these fused voxel features. As a result, the style supervision is anchored in 3D world coordinates, independent of the camera viewpoint, which avoids the view-dependent inconsistencies inherent in 2D image- or scene-level losses. For clarity, if we ignore the batch dimension and multi-level structure, the proposed 3D style loss is formalized in Algorithm 1.

**Algorithm 1: 3D Voxel-based AdaIN Style Loss**
**Inputs:**  Rendered features 𝓡, Style features 𝓢, 3D points 𝓟, Confidence 𝓒, Valid mask 𝓜 
**Output:**  3D style loss 𝓛
```pseudo
Initialize 𝓛 ← 0
Resize(𝓒, 𝓜, 𝓟) → match resolution of 𝓡
# Fuse all views into a voxel grid 
G ← VoxelizeAndFuse({𝓡,v}_{v=1..V},{𝓟,v}_{v=1..V},{𝓒,v}_{v=1..V},{𝓜,v}_{v=1..V})
# Compute BN statistics for two feature tensors
(μ_g, σ_g) ← MeanStd(G), (μ_s, σ_s) ← MeanStd(𝓢)
𝓛 ← 𝓛 + ‖μ_g − μ_s‖² + ‖σ_g − σ_s‖²
return 𝓛 = λ · 𝓛
```

In addition to improved consistency, **3D loss also enhances the artistic score**, as shown in Table 1. Together, these results indicate that enforcing style consistency at the voxel level leads ot more coherent stylized textures across views.

***Table 1. Artistic comparisons of different style loss designs***

| Style Loss | ArtScore↑ |
|:-----------|:----------:|
| Image loss | $5.96$ |
| Scene loss | $9.54$ |
| **3D loss** | $\mathbf{9.62}$ |

Regarding potential side effects, we have carefully evaluated a wide range of CO3D scenes, e.g., skateboards, donuts, pizzas, (see **Page 17-19, Figure 8-10**) under 50 diverse test styles (see **Page 22-23, Figure 14–15**), and we have not observed global color bleeding or loss of local style details that can be attributed to the voxel-level 3D style loss. For example, **Page 17 Figure 8** shows that the 3D style loss better preserves the wooden floor textures while achieving faithful stylization. We will release our implementations of all three style losses to enable further investigation by the community. As shown in **Page 18 Figure 9**, the 3D style loss is also able to stylize a larger portion of the table surface compared with the image-level loss. In **Page 19 Figure 10**, the seams on the tablecloth are well preserved under the 3D style loss, while they become partially distorted when using the image- or scene-level losses.

However, we have observed several failure cases where the overall ***Stylos*** is less effective. In particular, ***Stylos*** tends to perform noticeably worse on high-frequency, highly cluttered scenes, such as dense foliage and wire-like structures, and on style categories with strong global lighting shifts or extreme color palettes. In these cases, the model may struggle to maintain fine geometric detail or may over-saturate the stylized output. We have added multiple failure cases to the Appendix. More specifically, the failure cases can be grouped into three categories: 
* Failures caused by inaccurate scene reconstruction, such as missing geometric details or incorrect region colors, as shown in the revised paper **Page 20 Figure 11**; 
* Failures caused by generating colors that are absent from the original style images, as shown in the revised paper **Page 21 Figure 12**; 
* Failures caused by introducing blurry or over-smoothed style colors, as shown in the revised paper **Page 21 Figure 13**.


We have revised both the main paper and the appendix to include more detailed explanations about our loss designs with additional visual examples, enabling readers to better understand the differences among the three style losses and limitations of ***Stylos***. We expect more future work on improving the current version of ***Stylos***.

Thank you for highlighting this important point. We agree that the scalability limitations should be communicated more clearly. While ***Stylos*** is designed to support large numbers of input views, our scaling experiment indeed shows that performance begins to degrade when exceeding approximately 32 views per batch, with artifacts such as edge inconsistencies and reduced stability in the Gaussian representation. summary.value: The paper introduces StylOS, an efficient framework for view-consistent 3D style transfer using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). The main technical contribution is a single-forward inference model, built upon VGGT and AnySplat, that directly predicts the stylized 3DGS representation. This approach enables optimization-free, geometry-aware synthesis from unposed content views (from a single image to a multi-view collection) and a reference style image. By bypassing time-consuming per-scene optimization, StylOS achieves fast processing and superior generalization to unseen scenes and styles.

strengths.value:
1. **Single-Forward Efficiency**: The most compelling contribution is the ability to perform high-quality 3D style transfer in a single forward pass without per-scene optimization. This drastically reduces processing time and makes 3D stylization scalable for real-time or large-scale applications.

2. **Transformer Integration and Unposed Capability**: By utilizing a Transformer architecture (built upon VGGT) to directly predict the parameters of the stylized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, the method bypasses the traditional optimization pipeline and simultaneously enables robust handling of unposed content (single or multi-view). This significantly lowers the barrier to entry for users, as complex camera pose estimation is not required.

3. **Generalization and Robustness**: The method demonstrates excellent generalization capabilities across unseen content scenes, object categories, and style images, suggesting robust learning of disentangled style and geometry features.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Limited Technical Novelty in Overall Framework**: The overall conceptual framework of achieving fast, optimization-free 3D stylization by integrating a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model (VGGT/AnySplat) with cross-attention for style injection is highly similar to previous works like Styl3R (NeurIPS 2025, published on arXiv in May 2025), which uses Dust3R. While StylOS's integration of VGGT allows it to process a wider and more flexible range of input views, the core technical contribution of the idea of a single-forward 3D stylization framework is substantially weakened by this conceptual overlap. The authors should better address this overlap and clearly articulate how their specific implementation of the style injection and 3DGS prediction provides unique advantages over Styl3R's architecture.

2. **Style Fidelity vs. Optimization**: Although the speed advantage is clear, a deeper discussion or visual comparison is needed to evaluate the potential trade-off in style fidelity against state-of-the-art optimization-based 3D style transfer methods like 𝒢‐Style: Stylized Gaussian Splatting or ARF. Are there certain styles (e.g., fine-grained texture styles) where the feed-forward approach visibly struggles compared to optimization?

3. **Minor Formatting Concern (Font)**: It appears the authors may have modified the default font used in the ICLR style configuration.

questions.value:
1. **Style Control and Blending**: Can the authors demonstrate fine-grained control over the stylization process? Specifically:
a. Can the system adjust the content-style trade-off weight post-inference to control the strength of the stylistic transfer?
b. Can the model perform multi-style blending by interpolating or averaging the style embeddings from two or more distinct style images?

2. **Input and Output Resolution**: What is the range of resolutions for the input content views (single or multi-view) and the output rendering that the model is designed to support? Are there inherent limitations or scaling constraints related to the Transformer architecture or 3DGS representation density?

We have made every effort to conduct comprehensive experiments to further strengthen the persuasiveness of our method, which we believe helps clarify the reviewer’s concerns. 1. > Limited Technical Novelty in Overall Framework: The overall conceptual framework of achieving fast, optimization-free 3D stylization by integrating a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model (VGGT/AnySplat) with cross-attention for style injection is highly similar to previous works like Styl3R (NeurIPS 2025, published on arXiv in May 2025), which uses Dust3R. Thank you for raising the point regarding *Styl3R* [1], which has already been cited in our initial submission (lines 99 and 314). At the time of our submission, no code or reproducible models were available, and our method was developed independently, without access to their implementation details or design choices. Beyond the differences in backbone choice, our research focus and technical contributions are different from *Styl3R* [1], which will be clarified as follows.

(1) Our style injection mechanism follows the standard cross-attention formulation widely used in transformer-based 2D style transfer methods such as StyTr² [2], where content tokens serve as queries and style tokens serve as keys/values. Extending this to the 3D multi-view setting requires new design considerations regarding global attention, per-frame attention, and hybrid cross-attention. We build on the VGGT geometry aggregator, which employs hybrid cross-attention and empirically achieves better geometric stability. Our ablation study, as shown in the **following Table 1**, further shows that global-only cross-attention produces significantly better structural consistency than the other two strategies. *Styl3R* [1] does not discuss these distinctions or analyze style-injection mechanisms in detail.

We had not previously evaluated fine-grained style control, but we conducted additional experiments in response to the reviewer’s question (please see the visual results in the revised paper **Page 10, Figure 6**). This produces a continuous spectrum of outputs with varying degrees of stylization, demonstrating that our method can indeed provide post-inference control over the content–style trade-off. These results indicate that our approach enables both multi-style blending and adjustable stylization strength without requiring retraining or additional optimization.

The input resolution is constrained to 448 pixels on the longest side, with the aspect ratio randomized between 0.5 and 1.0. The stylized renderings are produced at the same resolution during training to ensure consistency between reconstruction and appearance transformation.

Because our backbone uses VGGT, the main architectural limitation is the model’s inability to process very long sequences of input views in a single forward pass, as standard self-attention scales quadratically with the number of image tokens.

For the 3DGS representation, the effective number of Gaussians is determined by the voxelization step, leading to a lower density than in pixel-wise Gaussian representations, which are usually used in a feedforward Gaussian model.

summary.value:
The paper introduces a feedforward stylized Gaussian method to achieve efficient, high-quality, and visually pleasing 3D scene reconstruction and stylization in a single step of model inference. The proposed approach is built upon VGGT, taking multi-view scene images and a style exemplar image as input. The model predicts the depth and camera poses for each view, while the predicted pixel Gaussian attributes are merged into voxels using confidence-based weights following the AnySplat framework. The results, as demonstrated in the figures and supplementary video, are remarkable.

This feedforward stylized Gaussian model has the potential to significantly impact the field. Artistic stylization, a cornerstone of human creativity throughout history, plays a vital role in bridging the technical and emotional aspects of visual representation. In the context of 3D world reconstruction, artistic stylization becomes even more critical, as it encapsulates the essence of reality through the lens of human emotion, emphasizing mood, character, and individuality. By enabling stylized 3D scene reconstruction without the need for test-time training, this model addresses a significant challenge and represents a major step forward in both technical and artistic innovation.

strengths.value:
The technical strengths of the paper can be summarized as follows:

1. This work is the first to achieve a stylized 3D world in a fully feedforward manner. From the early days of this field, StylizedNeRF introduced the concept of reconstructing 3D scenes using NeRF, accompanied by a conditional stylization module. While it generalized across styles, it required per-scene optimization. ARF, on the other hand, achieved superior results using a style-matching loss and a deferred backward strategy, but it was not generalized across scenes or styles. Both methods, being NeRF-based, faced limitations due to the high GPU demands during training, requiring solutions like mutual learning and deferred optimization to mitigate these challenges. Similarly, StyleRF was also restricted to per-scene optimization. 

   In the era of 3DGS, StylizedGS achieved impressive results in 3D stylization but remained constrained by per-scene fitting. This paper, however, marks a significant milestone by creating a stylized 3D world using a tuned foundation model like VGGT, combined with a generalized stylization module, enabling a fully feedforward pipeline. This eliminates the need for lengthy optimization processes. There is no more waiting hours to transform multi-view images into an artistic 3D world. This breakthrough paves the way for future research to focus on achieving even faster and higher-quality stylizations using similar feedforward approaches.

2. The results presented in the paper are both impressive and inspiring. The examples, particularly in the supplementary video, showcase how realistic 3D scenes can be transformed into artistic styles such as cartoon, sketch, and painting. The stylization maintains consistency across views without any flickering artifacts, which is a significant achievement. Moreover, obtaining such high-quality results in a single feedforward inference is truly remarkable and highlights the potential for real-time applications in this domain.

weaknesses.value:
1. The most significant contribution of this work is the introduction of a feedforward 3D stylization model, whose core advantages lie in faster inference and reduced memory usage. However, these critical metrics are not evaluated in the experiments. The paper should include a comparison of stylization time across prior works, from the earliest StylizedNeRF, ARF, and StyleRF to the more recent StyleGaussian and StylizedGaussian. For methods requiring per-scene fitting, the stylization time should account for both training and rendering times. Such comparisons would provide readers with a clearer perspective on how this work advances the field in terms of efficiency and practicality.

2. The comparison between NeRF-based and Gaussian-based stylization approaches is not adequately addressed. While StyleRF focuses on zero-shot stylization, its stylization quality is not the strongest. A detailed comparison with stylization examples from StylizedNeRF and similar NeRF-based methods is essential to highlight the advantages of the proposed approach. Moreover, StylizedGS, which outperforms StyleGS, should be included as the representative Gaussian-based stylization method in the comparisons. Incorporating these comparisons would strengthen the paper by demonstrating the superiority of the proposed method over both NeRF-based and Gaussian-based approaches.

> 2. Critical implementation details are missing regarding the voxelization operation: What is the voxel resolution? How are occlusions handled? What is the specific implementation of confidence weighting? Do these factors have a significant impact on the results?

Thank you for carefully reviewing our paper and bringing up these questions. We have added relevant implementation details to the paper. Specifically, the voxel size is set to 0.002. We do not explicitly model occlusions during voxelization; instead, occlusion effects are handled later in the pipeline through differentiable Gaussian rasterization ($\alpha$-compositing and depth ordering). Within each voxel, the Gaussian head predicts a per-Gaussian confidence value, which is converted into intra-voxel weights using a softmax. These weights are then used to compute confidence-weighted averages of all Gaussian attributes. This differentiable soft assignment stabilizes the clustering process and helps reduce redundancy among Gaussians. Finally, voxelization has a marginal effect on reconstruction accuracy but significantly improves scalability by slowing Gaussian count growth and reducing memory usage.

---

> 3. The weight parameters for each loss term are not provided.

Thank you for pointing this out. We have added the complete set of loss weights used in our experiments for clarity. Specifically, we use a style weight of 1.0, a content weight of 0.1, a CLIP consistency weight of 1.0, and a total variance regularization weight of 10.0.

---

> 4. The specific architecture of the Gaussian Adapter is not described in detail.

Thank you for highlighting the lack of architectural detail for the Gaussian Adapter. We have added a description of this adapter to the appendix. Specifically, the adapter splits the raw Gaussian parameters from the Gaussian head into scale, rotation, and spherical-harmonics components; applies softplus-based scale regularization and quaternion normalization; and constructs full 3D covariance matrices.

---

> 5. There is insufficient discussion on which scene types or style categories the method performs poorly on.

Thank you for raising this point. We have expanded our discussion to clarify the scenarios where the method is less effective. In particular, ***Stylos*** tends to perform noticeably worse on high-frequency, highly cluttered scenes (e.g., dense foliage, wire-like structures) and on style categories with strong global lighting shifts or extreme color palettes. In these cases, the model may struggle to maintain fine geometric detail or may over-saturate the stylized output. We have added multiple failure cases to the Appendix. More specifically, the failure cases can be grouped into three categories: 
* Failures caused by inaccurate scene reconstruction, such as missing geometric details or incorrect region colors, as shown in the **Page 20 Figure 11**; 
* Failures caused by generating colors that are absent from the original style images, as shown in the **Page 21 Figure 12**; 
* Failures caused by introducing blurry or over-smoothed style colors, as shown in the **Page 21 Figure 13**.

> 6. Why does global cross-attention not only improve style consistency but also enhance geometric fidelity? This seems counterintuitive and requires deeper analysis.

Thanks for pointing out this valuable point. To answer the question, let us review the architecture and training strategy of ***Stylos***. (1) Basically, ***Stylos*** consists of a style pathway which contributes to the color information for the predicted 3DGS representation, and a content pathway for the other 3DGS parameters. In the style pathway, we introduce a style aggregator with cross-attention to entangle the content and style tokens. (2) Our training pipeline consists of two stages. Stage 1 focuses on 3D scene reconstruction, where a random content view is used as the style reference; Stage 2 performs actual stylization using a real artistic style image. 

When designing  ***Stylos***, it is therefore essential to verify that introducing content-style cross-attention in the style aggregator does not harm the image quality of the rendered multi-view rgbs during Stage 1. Similar discussions about the importance of appearance-geometry entanglement in 3DGS and the potential effect of appearance to the final rendered outputs could be found in previous work such as ReGS [5], Texture-GS [6] and multiple 3DGS-based works.

To this end, we compare three content–style coupling mechanisms (global, frame, and both) by calculating PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS between the rendered multi-view rgbs and their corresponding ground-thruth after Stage 1 training, using the first content view as the style reference. Interestingly, as shown in the **following Table 4**, the global-only variant achieves the best reconstruction accuracy and outperforms the hybrid method. 2. We start from the image-level style loss, which aligns statistics (mean and variance) per view independently, to the scene-level style loss, which aligns statistics considering all input views per scene, and finally the voxel-level 3d style loss, which aligns statistics in the aggregated voxel space. Our quantitative comparisons (**Page 7 Table 2**) and qualitative comparisons (**Page 8 Figure 3**, **Page 17-19 Figure 8-10**) clearly demonstrate the advantages of the 3D style loss over the other variants.
3. The paper presents Stylos, a method for 3D stylization conditioned on a reference style image, applicable to both unposed single-view and multi-view inputs. Stylos builds on the VGGT architecture, leverages 3D Gaussians as the scene representation, and performs style transfer in a single forward pass, achieving competitive visual quality with high efficiency. The initial reviews were very positive, and all reviewers agreed that the paper meets the acceptance bar. Reviewers praised the new capabilities enabled by Stylos and found the empirical results convincing. The minor concerns raised by reviewers were subsequently addressed in the rebuttal.

After carefully considering the paper, reviews, and rebuttal, the AC recommends acceptance.
